raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic systolic heart-failure syndrome presenting toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) typically <45% and no alternative explanation for heart failure [1–4]. It remains diagnostically challenging because dyspnea, edema, fatigue, and tachycardia overlap with normal late pregnancy; echocardiography is therefore central to diagnosis, risk stratification, and follow-up [1,4]. Contemporary definitions have relaxed the historical “last month to 5 months postpartum” window because clinically similar cases may present earlier in late gestation or later postpartum [2,3].

The incidence of PPCM varies markedly by geography, ancestry, ascertainment, and case definition. Internationally, the highest reported rates occur in parts of Africa and Haiti, whereas lower rates are reported in Japan and some European cohorts [17]. In North America, PPCM is more common among Black women and is associated with older maternal age, multiparity, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and multifetal gestation [14–16]. A large U.S. inpatient analysis suggested increasing incidence and substantial in-hospital morbidity, including cardiogenic shock, thromboembolism, device implantation, and mechanical circulatory support [15]. Population-based data also show important long-term mortality, emphasizing that PPCM is not uniformly reversible [16].

Pathobiology is heterogeneous and probably reflects interaction between genetic susceptibility and late-pregnancy vascular-hormonal stress [2,3]. Experimental models implicate oxidative stress, cathepsin-D–mediated cleavage of prolactin into an antiangiogenic 16-kDa fragment, endothelial injury, and microvascular dysfunction [9,10]. A complementary pathway involves angiogenic imbalance: reduced myocardial proangiogenic reserve and increased placental soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1), particularly in preeclampsia, may impair cardiac microvasculature [8,13]. Downstream, miR-146a appears to mediate antiangiogenic and cardiometabolic effects and has been proposed as a disease biomarker [11]. Genetic studies have strengthened the “two-hit” model: truncating variants in TTN and other dilated-cardiomyopathy genes occur in a clinically meaningful subset, supporting consideration of genetic counseling and testing, especially with family history, severe presentation, arrhythmias, or incomplete recovery [12,13].

Clinically, PPCM ranges from mild congestion to fulminant cardiogenic shock. Baseline LVEF, left ventricular size, right ventricular dysfunction, timing of presentation, and treatment access all influence recovery [5–7]. In the IPAC cohort, many North American patients improved, but severe baseline LV dysfunction and greater LV dilatation predicted persistent impairment [7]. The ESC EORP registry showed global heterogeneity: at 6 months, recovery to LVEF ≥50% occurred in fewer than half of women, while death or persistent severe LV dysfunction remained common [6]. Biomarker substudies suggest sFlt1 and related vascular mediators correlate with severity, but no biomarker yet replaces imaging for clinical decision-making [8].

Management requires a cardio-obstetric team. During pregnancy, therapy includes diuretics for congestion, beta-blockers, hydralazine–nitrate vasodilation when needed, and careful anticoagulation when LVEF is very low or thrombus is present; angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are generally avoided until after delivery because of fetal safety concerns [1–4]. After delivery, guideline-directed heart-failure therapy should be initiated and titrated, with attention to breastfeeding compatibility, contraception, blood pressure, renal function, and thromboembolic risk [3,18]. Bromocriptine, a prolactin inhibitor, is biologically plausible and supported by a South African proof-of-concept study and a German randomized trial showing favorable LV recovery signals, but it suppresses lactation and requires anticoagulation; practice varies pending larger outcome trials [22,23].

Advanced presentations demand early transfer to centers capable of invasive hemodynamic monitoring, temporary mechanical circulatory support, durable LV assist devices, and transplantation [4]. Because recovery can occur late, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator decisions are usually deferred unless arrhythmia risk is compelling; wearable defibrillators or temporary strategies may be considered during the recovery window. Cardiac magnetic resonance can help exclude myocarditis, infarction, or infiltrative disease, evaluate thrombus, and characterize tissue, although its prognostic role in PPCM remains evolving [25–27]. A subset progresses to transplantation; transplant outcomes are acceptable but PPCM recipients may have distinctive sensitization and rejection considerations [28–30].

Long-term care should continue beyond apparent recovery. Meta-analysis suggests only about half of patients achieve durable myocardial recovery, and mortality, transplantation, LV assist device use, and relapse remain important late outcomes [24]. Subsequent pregnancy is the most consequential counseling issue. Persistent LV dysfunction before conception confers high risk of relapse, irreversible deterioration, and death; even women with normalized LVEF have measurable recurrence risk [18–21]. Preconception assessment should include symptoms, echocardiography, medication review, and shared decision-making; if pregnancy proceeds, close surveillance through pregnancy and at least 6 months postpartum is essential. Future priorities include equitable early diagnosis, genotype-informed risk stratification, lactation-compatible disease-specific therapy, and trials powered for maternal and infant outcomes.
